ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: When one household has trouble and a hundred are busy describes disturbance spreading through an entire community.
EvidenceBody: Yunju applies the proverb to the Manjusri–Mahakasyapa case before Shakyamuni; Dahui repeats it inside Miyun's later appraisal, while other records redeploy the same shared-burden image.

DraftEvidence.ZenBend: The proverb spreads one household’s disturbance across a whole neighborhood, fitting both Yunju’s case appraisal and later critiques of cascading trouble.
DraftEvidence.CounterexampleOrLimit: The proverb marks repercussions that mobilize many beyond the household directly involved.

ComparedThings: when one household has trouble, a hundred households are busy
the retained dialogue, sermon, verse, and appraisal uses
DifferentThingTest.Reason: Whether aimed at Manjusri’s case or a teacher’s inherited device, the one-to-hundred expansion expresses communal repercussions.

DraftEvidence.AliasRationale: The alias keeps the disproportion between one troubled house and a hundred busy ones.

ModifierControls.Finding: The numerical contrast carries the widening effect from a single locus to many responders.

FamilyControls.Finding: Domestic-event phrases without 百家忙 lack the proverb’s spreading consequence.
